chunks: "Think of a half-bridge as a switch that connects the output either to the supply or to ground.
If I flip it fast, with the top switch on for a fraction D of the time, the motor sees an average of D times the supply, so duty cycle sets speed.
The motor winding is an inductor, so it smooths the pulses into a nearly steady current. The important part is what happens when the top switch turns off.

The inductor current can't stop, so the output node swings down until the bottom switch's body diode catches it, or until I turn the bottom FET on, and the current freewheels through the motor and that path.
That's why a half-bridge always has two devices: one pushes current in, the other gives it somewhere to go. An H-bridge is two half-bridges with the motor between them.
If the left leg is high and the right leg is low, the current goes one way; swap them and it reverses.

For speed control I can PWM one leg while holding the other low, which gives slow decay and low ripple, or PWM both legs in opposite phase so that 50% duty means zero average voltage, which gives bidirectional control from a single signal.
Throughout, I add a bit of dead time on every leg so the top and bottom never conduct together."
